title: SpaceX claims Starlink Mobile will be better than AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
gist: SpaceX executives said on the earnings call that they plan to build a terrestrial Starlink Mobile network using small femtocells (not big towers) on top of existing Starlink dishes, powered by 65 MHz of spectrum bought from EchoStar, aiming to take a large share of the roughly $600 billion combined AT&T/Verizon/T-Mobile market — but analysts are skeptical the spectrum and capacity are sufficient to compete without an MVNO deal, and the plan lands the same day SpaceX's AI capex spooked investors.

insights.claim: SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said on the earnings call that spectrum purchased from EchoStar includes terrestrial components, and that SpaceX 'definitely' intends to build out a terrestrial network alongside its satellite capacity to make Starlink Mobile 'exactly what you want it to be.'
insights.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: This marks a strategic shift from SpaceX merely supplementing carrier networks via satellite to building a competing terrestrial cellular network — a direct new threat vector to AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile that changes SpaceX's addressable market.
insights.quote: The spectrum that we purchased from EchoStar does have terrestrial components, so we definitely intend to build out the terrestrial component.

insights.claim: Shotwell said AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile collectively generate roughly $600 billion a year in revenue, and that she anticipates SpaceX will 'acquire quite a few of their customers' because Starlink will eliminate dead zones and perform better during natural disasters.
insights.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: A $600B combined addressable market gives a scale reference for how large a prize SpaceX is targeting; even a small single-digit percentage share captured would be a meaningful new SpaceX revenue stream.
insights.quote: I anticipate us to be able to acquire quite a few of their customers because I think our service will be better.

insights.claim: Shotwell said SpaceX will start flying next-generation Starlink mobile satellites next year (2027) and begin providing service by the end of next year.
insights.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: A concrete 2027-2028 timeline for next-gen mobile satellite service is a trackable milestone for whether SpaceX's terrestrial-mobile ambitions materialize on schedule.

themes.theme: Femtocell architecture: small stations, not big towers

insights.claim: Rather than building large cell towers, SpaceX plans to deploy 'little femtocells around the country,' putting a cellular base station on the same gear that holds a Starlink broadband dish, according to Shotwell.
insights.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: This is a fundamentally different and potentially far cheaper capex model than traditional cell tower buildouts, leveraging SpaceX's existing installed base of home/business Starlink dishes as de facto network infrastructure — a structural cost advantage thesis worth testing against actual buildout costs as they emerge.

insights.claim: Musk said existing Starlink antennas on the roofs of homes and businesses have a clear view for providing connectivity directly to cellphones on the ground, and that this could provide connectivity 'probably better and higher bandwidth than what is currently available from cellular providers.'
insights.speaker: Elon Musk (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: This is Musk's core technical bet — that distributed rooftop antennas beat centralized towers for coverage and bandwidth — an unproven claim investors should treat skeptically pending independent network performance testing.
insights.quote: Starlink antennas are located on the roofs of houses and businesses. They’ve got a clear view for providing connectivity directly to cellphones on the ground.

insights.claim: Shotwell declined to disclose the capex required to build the terrestrial network, saying SpaceX has 'a lot of really kind of great and new ideas' for doing it in a capex-efficient way, deploying stations incrementally rather than spending billions upfront on low-band spectrum before deployment.
insights.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: Withholding capex guidance on a major new network buildout — especially the same day SpaceX's AI capex spooked investors — is a red flag for investors trying to model SpaceX's total infrastructure spending trajectory.
insights.quote: I don’t want to talk about the CapEx for building out the terrestrial, because we have a lot of really kind of great and new ideas for how we’re going to do that, and I think it will be quite CapEx-efficient.

insights.claim: SpaceX is buying 65 MHz of nationwide spectrum licenses from EchoStar between 1.695 GHz and 2.2 GHz, including both terrestrial and satellite deployment rights; the FCC approved the deal in May, though the full transaction requires additional non-US regulatory approvals and is scheduled to complete by November 30, 2027 (with SpaceX gaining interim access via a temporary trust).
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The regulatory completion timeline (through late 2027) is a concrete gating factor for when SpaceX can fully exploit the spectrum, and the multi-jurisdiction approval requirement is an execution risk to monitor.

insights.claim: New Street Research analyst David Barden said it 'makes no sense for SpaceX to try to replicate what terrestrial players have built over 30 years with 1,000 MHz between them, with 65 MHz,' noting roughly 1.1 GHz of licensed spectrum was allocated to mobile operators as of the beginning of last year per CTIA.
insights.speaker: David Barden (quoted by Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: A direct analyst bear case with a specific spectrum-ratio comparison (65 MHz vs. ~1,000+ MHz held by incumbents) quantifies exactly how large the capacity gap is between SpaceX's ambitions and the physical spectrum resources it currently controls.
insights.quote: It makes no sense for SpaceX to try to replicate what terrestrial players have built over 30 years with 1,000 MHz between them, with 65 MHz.

insights.claim: Telecom analyst Craig Moffett said that unless Starlink secures an MVNO (Mobile Virtual Network Operator) agreement from one of the existing carriers to provide baseline coverage, it's 'extraordinarily challenging' to imagine a direct-to-consumer Starlink service competitive with carrier services within the next five years.
insights.speaker: Craig Moffett (quoted by Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: A named analyst setting a specific five-year skepticism window on SpaceX's direct-to-consumer mobile ambitions absent an MVNO deal is a concrete bear-case timeline investors can use to judge whether SpaceX's rollout is ahead or behind expectations.
insights.quote: Unless Starlink can secure an MVNO (Mobile Virtual Network Operator) agreement from one of the carriers, which would provide a baseline of coverage, it’s extraordinarily challenging to imagine a direct-to-consumer service.

insights.claim: Shotwell said the current Starlink Mobile system uses only 5 MHz through partnerships with telco providers, and that adding the 65 MHz from EchoStar plus expanded satellite capabilities would together make the system about 100 times better than it is now.
insights.speaker: Gwynne Shotwell (via Jon Brodkin)
insights.so_what: A claimed 100x capability improvement is a specific, falsifiable benchmark to test against real-world Starlink Mobile performance data as the buildout progresses.

insights.claim: Starlink has deployed about 650 Direct to Cell (D2C) satellites under existing authorizations and is seeking FCC approval to launch up to 15,000 next-generation mobile satellites, with next-gen direct-to-device service targeted to begin by late 2027 and thousands of upgraded cellular satellites launched by the end of 2028, per a SpaceX filing with the Canadian government.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The gap between 650 currently deployed satellites and a 15,000-satellite target reveals the scale of buildout still required — a useful benchmark to track SpaceX's launch cadence against its stated D2C roadmap.

insights.claim: Starlink's existing home Internet service already shows capacity limits in practice, with the company charging higher prices in congested areas and imposing 'demand surcharges' of up to $1,500.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Real-world evidence that Starlink's existing satellite capacity is already strained in high-demand areas undercuts the claim that a mobile buildout will automatically deliver unconstrained nationwide capacity comparable to terrestrial carriers.

insights.claim: T-Mobile has already partnered with SpaceX for satellite supplementation, while AT&T and Verizon have similar deals with satellite company AST SpaceMobile; all three major carriers recently announced a joint venture to pool spectrum and help non-SpaceX satellite providers reach more customers through a unified platform.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The big three carriers coordinating on a joint venture that favors a non-SpaceX satellite partner (AST SpaceMobile) signals a defensive alliance forming specifically to counter SpaceX's growing independence and competitive threat — relevant for AST SpaceMobile's competitive positioning.

insights.claim: The three major carriers' stock prices fell the same day SpaceX announced its intention to compete more directly against them via Starlink Mobile.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: An immediate negative market reaction in incumbent carrier stocks on the mere announcement of intent (without a live competing service yet) shows the market is already pricing in credible long-term competitive threat from SpaceX.
